<reflection>
After two experiments, the fitting results show that M8 and M6 are the best-fitting models, with nearly identical negative log-likelihood (NLL) values. M7 is slightly worse, followed by a cluster of mechanisms (M1, M2, M10, etc.) that are also close. M4 and M5 are clear outliers with large positive NLL and can be ruled out. The second experiment (low catalyst) did not significantly separate the top candidates; the NLL differences remain small. The aim of the second turn was to probe catalyst concentration dependence, which provided some discrimination (e.g., M3 worsened relative to others) but not enough to narrow down the set decisively. We need an experiment that can amplify differences among the remaining plausible mechanisms.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
I propose an experiment with lower substrate concentration (0.5 M) and moderate catalyst (0.01 M), with no initial product. This condition explores the kinetic regime where substrate is not in large excess relative to catalyst (though still 50-fold excess). It will help discriminate mechanisms based on their substrate binding affinity and saturation behavior. For example, mechanisms with dimerization (M2, M3) or activation (M6, M8) may exhibit different apparent Michaelis constants. Mechanisms with substrate inhibition (M7, M11, M16) might show deviations at higher substrate, but here we are going lower, so we might see linear vs. hyperbolic dependence. This design avoids extreme conditions (e.g., very high substrate that saturates all mechanisms or very low substrate that yields negligible conversion) and provides a new dimension of variation (substrate concentration) orthogonal to the previous experiments (which varied catalyst concentration at fixed high substrate). By measuring the progress curve at lower substrate, we can better constrain the substrate dependence of the rate law, which should help differentiate among the top candidates and the cluster of deactivation mechanisms simultaneously.
</hypothesis>
